claims.text: The corrosion performance of untreated Q235 steel in saline humid environments is governed by the temperature-dependent integrity of its native oxide film.
At room temperature, the native oxide film on Q235 steel remains relatively intact.
An intact oxide film impedes chloride-ion penetration.
Exposure at approximately 60°C thermally degrades the native oxide film, making it porous and discontinuous.
Thermally induced oxide-film porosity and possible spallation enhance chloride-ion penetration.
Enhanced chloride penetration increases localized corrosion and pitting.
As-received, pre-exposure Q235 steel has an intact native oxide layer.
Samples exposed to saline humidity at 60°C will have a higher corrosion rate than samples exposed at 25°C.
Samples exposed at 60°C will develop a greater pitting density than samples exposed at 25°C.
Samples exposed at 60°C will develop deeper localized attack than samples exposed at 25°C.
At 25°C, corrosion will be more uniform and slower because the oxide film remains relatively intact.
The proposed mechanism applies to Q235 steel in environments dominated by saline humidity.
Acidic conditions and mechanical stresses are outside the proposed model's boundary conditions.
A controlled comparison will use 3.5% NaCl humid atmospheres at 25°C and 60°C while holding humidity, sample geometry, and exposure time constant.
Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in corrosion rate and pitting at 60°C, or observation of comparable oxide-film integrity at both temperatures, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is Q235 steel under ambient conditions without saline or temperature stress, but the prediction and falsification experiment use the 25°C saline-humidity group as the reference. The operative untreated reference is therefore inconsistent across fields.
